angle: AI can't brainstorm from nothing. Humans bring the first 2-3 ideas and Claude gets you to 10
post_first_line: Humans bring 2 or 3 ideas. AI does the rest.
linkedin_post:
Humans bring 2 or 3 ideas. AI does the rest.

AI gets you the rest, but only if you start the right way.

A couple weeks ago, Sarah came by our office and we ran a brainstorming session on how we could be betting more broadly as a team.

We went through every channel we run today, where we're seeing success, and where we're not. We left with a bunch of ideas on what to improve.

AI can amplify a session like that. But the kernels of insight still need to come from people.

The first 2 or 3 ideas are what give Claude something to work with. From there, it can help you get to 7 through 10.

Ask AI to brainstorm from a blank page and you get generic output. Give it a few real ideas from people who know the business and it has something to build on.

Humans plant the seeds. Claude helps you grow the garden.

Where do your best ideas come from today?

lesson.title: Humans seed the ideas, AI scales them

The first 2 or 3 ideas give Claude the context to get you to 7 through 10.
Reviewing what's working and what's not across channels gives the session real material.
lesson.exercise: Before your next brainstorm, write down 2 or 3 ideas of your own about a channel or problem. Give them to Claude as context and ask it to extend the list to 10. Then compare that to what a blank-prompt request gives you.

angle: Feeling behind on AI? Start with small chats, then build your first skill
post_first_line: Months of using AI tools internally. Still anxious.
linkedin_post:
Months of using AI tools internally. Still anxious.

The anxiety is real, and I think it's coming from the wrong place.

A lot of people feel behind right now. What should I be doing? How is this supposed to work? Those questions stall people before they start.

My advice: start small. Don't force yourself into some crazy complicated use case.

Run a few chats in Claude. Then move into building your first skill.

It doesn't need to be perfect. The intuition comes from trying things, not from reading about them as a third party.

Nobody gets caught up by reading another thread about AI. You get caught up by opening the tool and messing around.

What's the first thing you'd try this week?

takeaways: Anxiety about being behind is common, and it comes from not knowing where to start.
Skip the complicated use case. Begin with simple chats in Claude, then build your first skill.
Intuition is built by trying things yourself, not by reading about them as a third party.
lesson.exercise: Open Claude today and run three chats on real work you're already doing. Then pick one repeatable task and turn it into your first skill, even if it's imperfect.

angle: Build the lead magnet, not a beautiful page: always include a CTA
post_first_line: Built a full page concept in under 30 seconds.
linkedin_post:
Built a full page concept in under 30 seconds.

But the speed isn't the part worth copying.

Sarah Charlton built a page with a hero image, a toggle, a headline, customer quotes, and inputs Quentin asked for. It looked polished, and it took less than 30 seconds.

The first thing Sarah added was a talk to sales button. Sarah's reasoning: you've always got to have a CTA.

The page exists to be a lead magnet, not a beautiful page.

Sarah also had the page email results to visitors, with a second CTA at the end. So there are two chances to convert: one up top, one after the value is delivered.

When building a page takes seconds, the design stops being the hard part. The hard part is deciding what the page is supposed to make someone do.

What's the CTA on your last lead magnet?
carousel: Slide 1: This page took under 30 seconds to build.
Slide 2: Sarah Charlton started with the CTA, not the design.
Slide 3: A talk to sales button goes on every page.
Slide 4: The goal is a lead magnet, not a beautiful page.
Slide 5: Hero image, toggle, headline, inputs, customer quotes.
Slide 6: Results get emailed to the visitor.
Slide 7: That email carries a second CTA.
Slide 8: Fast builds make the conversion goal the real work.

lesson.title: Build the lead magnet, not a beautiful page
takeaways: Put a CTA on the page first, then design around it.
A lead magnet is judged by whether it converts, not how it looks.
Emailing results to visitors creates a second CTA moment.
lesson.exercise: Open your current lead magnet page and count the CTAs. If there are fewer than two, add one at the top and one in the results email.

caption: Always include a CTA

angle: We've never posted a LinkedIn post straight out of AI, and here's why
linkedin_post:
Zero AI-written posts. Ever.

I've written on LinkedIn for the past couple years, and there's one rule I've never broken.

We have never taken a post straight out of AI and published it. Not once.

It's just not good enough. It isn't interesting.

AI doesn't have the taste and care that someone good at marketing has. It doesn't understand what's happening in the zeitgeist right now, or how people are feeling about things.

And I'm not confident it's going to take a lot to close that gap. But today, that's one area where I don't personally get any leverage out of it.

I use AI plenty elsewhere. Writing the final post isn't where it earns its keep for me.

Where do you draw the line with AI?

Slide 8: For now, writing posts is where I get no leverage.

lesson.title: Taste is the part AI can't write for you yet
takeaways: AI-generated posts miss the taste and care a good marketer brings.
AI doesn't grasp the zeitgeist or how people feel about things right now.
The gap may close soon, but today it's still a real limit on posting.
lesson.exercise: Take your last AI-drafted post and mark every line that shows no awareness of what your audience is feeling this week. Rewrite those lines yourself before publishing.

angle: Don't ask AI to invent your ROI math. Bring the logic, let it build the page
linkedin_post:
12 pages of size 12 font.

That was the ROI calculator Sarah Charlton started with.

Sarah Charlton's rule for AI and ROI: you don't tell AI to figure out the ROI on Unify. That isn't something you can delegate, and you don't want AI running that logic for you.

So the logic came from Quentin, who put together a calculator alongside a detailed diagram. It was 12 pages of very detailed instructions.

The session was only 15 minutes. So Sarah asked Claude to turn it into something much simpler that could be built in the time available.

Claude came back with a really simple calculator. That simplified Unify ROI calculator is what the session used.

The split is clear. Humans own the math and the reasoning. AI handles the build and the simplification.

If the logic is wrong, a nicer page won't fix it.

Where do you draw the line with AI?

Slide 2: ROI logic isn't something you can delegate to AI.
Slide 3: Quentin's original calculator ran 12 pages of detailed instructions.
Slide 4: The session had only 15 minutes to build.
Slide 5: So Sarah asked Claude to simplify it.
Slide 6: Claude turned it into a really simple calculator.
Slide 7: You bring the logic. AI builds the page.

lesson.title: Own the logic, let AI build the page
takeaways: ROI reasoning is yours to define. Don't delegate it to AI.
Detailed source logic can be simplified by AI to fit your time limit.
Start with a human-built framework, then ask AI to make it buildable.
lesson.exercise: Write down your ROI logic in a few plain steps. Then ask AI to turn only those steps into a simple calculator.

caption: Don't let AI invent your ROI

angle: Sales isn't AI vs. human anymore. AI is table stakes and selling stays human-to-human
post_first_line: Sarah Charlton heard a take worth pausing on.
linkedin_post:
Sarah Charlton heard a take worth pausing on.

The AI-versus-human debate in sales may already be over.

A year or two ago, the story was that AI would replace sales. That story has faded. The current one is sales plus AI, where AI absorbs the research and administration.

Sarah's view: AI is now table stakes. Having it isn't the edge anymore.

The more interesting question is how the best sellers use AI to get leverage. Selling is inherently human-to-human, and that isn't going anywhere.

So the gap won't come from who uses AI. It will come from what sellers do with the time AI gives back.

Where has AI freed up the most time on your team?
carousel: Slide 1: Sales is no longer AI versus human.
Slide 2: The AI-replaces-sales story has faded in the past year or two.
Slide 3: Now it's sales plus AI, with AI absorbing research and admin.
Slide 4: AI is table stakes. It's no longer an edge.
Slide 5: The best sellers use AI to get leverage.
Slide 6: Selling is inherently human-to-human. That isn't going anywhere.
Slide 7: Use AI for the grunt work. Spend the time on buyers.

lesson.title: AI Is Table Stakes. Selling Stays Human.
takeaways: The narrative has shifted from AI replacing sales to sales plus AI.
AI should absorb research and administration work.
The best sellers use AI for leverage, while the selling itself stays human-to-human.
lesson.exercise: List your team's weekly tasks and mark each as research/admin or buyer-facing. Hand the research/admin ones to AI, and use the time saved on more human conversations.
